title: A&P Applied to Office Tasks

sections.learningObjectives:
- Relate anatomy and physiology knowledge to coding and laboratory work.
- Apply anatomy and physiology knowledge to patient education and communication.
- Recognize body-system references in records and orders.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Imagine everyone agrees to stand the same way for a photo before describing 'up, down, front, and back.' That shared starting pose is the anatomical position.

### Question 2

The heart and the tubes that carry blood around your body are one team — that team is the cardiovascular system.

### Question 3

Think of 'superior' as 'higher up, like the top shelf.' So something superior to the belly button is above it.

### Question 4

'Posterior' sounds like 'post' or 'behind,' so it means the back side — here, the back of the knee.

### Question 5

Stand up straight: your heart is in the middle, and your lungs are on either side. Things near the middle are 'medial.'

### Question 6

On an arm, 'proximal' means closer to the shoulder where the arm attaches — so up near the elbow for a forearm wound.

### Question 7

Homeostasis is like a thermostat keeping a room at the same temperature even when it gets hotter or colder outside.

### Question 8

Draw a plus sign over the belly button: the upper-right box holds the liver and gallbladder.

### Question 9

Your chest is like a protected box that holds your heart and lungs — that box is the thoracic cavity.

### Question 10

Your skin, hair, and nails are your built-in raincoat and armor — together they are the integumentary system.

### Question 11

Think of a big filing cabinet sorted by body parts. To file a 'rash' card in the right drawer, you have to know a rash is a skin problem.

### Question 12

'Myo' means muscle and 'cardial' means heart — so 'myocardial infarction' is a problem with the heart muscle.

### Question 13

'Cerebro' is the word for brain, so a cerebrovascular accident is a problem in the brain, not the heart or lungs.

### Question 14

'Derm' means skin, like a dermatologist is a skin doctor. So dermatitis is a skin problem.

### Question 15

'Nephro' is a fancy word for kidney, so nephritis means an angry, swollen kidney.

### Question 16

'Hepat' is the word for liver, so hepatitis means the liver is inflamed.

### Question 17

'Pneumo' has to do with air and the lungs, so pneumonia is a sickness in the lungs.

### Question 18

'Gastr' means stomach, so gastritis is an upset, inflamed stomach.

### Question 19

'Cyst' here means bladder, so cystitis is an irritated bladder.

### Question 20

'Osteo' means bone and 'arthro' means joint — so osteoarthritis is wear-and-tear in a joint like the knee.

### Question 21

'Ot' means ear, so otitis media is an ear infection in the middle part of the ear.

### Question 22

The conjunctiva is the clear covering of the eye, so conjunctivitis is 'pink eye.'

### Question 23

If you have a cut on your right arm, the doctor's note must say 'right arm,' because 'left' and 'right' get filed in different slots.

### Question 24

A sudden stomachache that comes on fast is 'acute,' like a fire alarm; a problem that hangs around for months is 'chronic,' like a slow leak.

### Question 25

'-itis' is like the word 'irritated' — it tells you a body part is red, swollen, and angry.

### Question 26

Your pancreas is like the sugar manager of your body; a blood glucose test checks how well that manager is working.

### Question 27

Lipids are fats floating in your blood. Too much can clog the pipes (blood vessels), so this test checks your heart's plumbing.

### Question 28

Hemoglobin is the red, oxygen-carrying part of blood. Low hemoglobin means fewer red 'delivery trucks' carrying oxygen.

### Question 29

A urinalysis looks at your pee, which is made by the kidneys — so it checks the body's water-filtering system.

### Question 30

The liver is the body's cleanup crew; ALT and AST are like smoke alarms that go off when liver cells are hurt.

### Question 31

TSH is a message the brain sends to your thyroid, the gland that controls your energy; the test checks if that message and gland are working right.

### Question 32

Your kidneys are filters that clean waste from your blood. Creatinine and BUN measure how well those filters are working.

### Question 33

Troponin is like a special alarm that only rings when the heart muscle is hurt, helping doctors spot a heart problem.

### Question 34

A1c is like a report card for blood sugar over the past few months, not just one day.

### Question 35

Imagine turning in two homework papers with no names — the teacher can't tell whose is whose. Specimen labels do the same job for the lab.

### Question 36

Fasting means your stomach takes a break — only water — so the test sees your body's true baseline, not your last meal.

### Question 37

White blood cells are your body's soldiers; more soldiers show up when there's an infection to fight.

### Question 38

'Fecal' means poop and 'occult' means hidden — this test hunts for blood you can't see in the stool.

### Question 39

A culture is like planting a sample to see what germs grow, then testing which medicine can knock those germs out.

### Question 40

Sodium and potassium are like tiny electrical helpers that let your nerves and muscles 'plug in' and work, while also balancing your body's water.

### Question 41

Vital signs are the four 'check-engine lights' of the body: temperature, pulse, breathing, and blood pressure.

### Question 42

Your body works like a thermostat to keep its temperature just right; taking your temperature checks that thermostat.

### Question 43

Each 'thump' you feel at your wrist is your heart squeezing blood through your arteries — that's your pulse.

### Question 44

Counting how many times someone breathes in a minute tells you how their lungs and breathing are doing.

### Question 45

Blood pressure is how hard your blood pushes against your artery walls, like water pressure in a hose.

### Question 46

A pulse oximeter is a little clip that reads how 'full of oxygen' your blood is, like a gas gauge for your body.

### Question 47

A blood pressure of 120 over 80 is the 'just right' reading most adults aim for.

### Question 48

Each vital sign is a window into one part of the body: the pulse peeks at the heart, breathing peeks at the lungs, and so on.

### Question 49

If a smoke alarm goes off, you don't ignore it or paint over it — you tell someone. Abnormal vital signs work the same way.

### Question 50

Pain is like someone telling you their tummy hurts — you write down exactly what they say and how bad they say it is, because only they can feel it.

### Question 51

BMI compares how much a person weighs to how tall they are, giving a rough idea of whether weight is in a healthy range.

### Question 52

The spot on your wrist where you can feel your heartbeat is called the radial pulse — it's the easiest place to count.

### Question 53

'Pyrexia' is just the doctor-word for a fever, when your body runs hotter than normal.

### Question 54

If people know you're counting their breaths, they might breathe differently — so you quietly count for a full minute while they relax.

### Question 55

Imagine a garden hose: the harder the water pushes against the inside, the higher the pressure. Your arteries work the same way with blood.

### Question 56

When you drink water, your body can fill up the 'sample cup' more easily, and the pee isn't too strong and dark.

### Question 57

Eating is like stirring sugar into a cup of tea right before tasting it — fasting lets the test measure the 'plain tea' baseline.

### Question 58

An X-ray is like a quick black-and-white photo of your bones; an MRI is like a super-detailed picture of your soft parts, like muscles and the brain.

### Question 59

Your heart is like the engine pump that keeps blood moving around your body, delivering the good stuff your cells need.

### Question 60

Having high blood sugar means there's extra sugar floating in your blood — like too much sugar stirred into your drink — and your doctor will talk with you about it.

### Question 61

Stopping medicine is a decision for the doctor, not something you guess at — so you remind the patient to follow the plan and ask the provider.

### Question 62

Cholesterol is a fatty substance your body needs a little of, but too much is like gunk building up inside a pipe.

### Question 63

Before measuring, you sit calmly like a car idling at a red light, so the reading shows your body's true resting pressure.

### Question 64

Think of digestion as a long slide where food is taken apart into tiny building blocks your body can use, and the leftovers leave as waste.

### Question 65

Your lungs are like balloons that pull in fresh oxygen when you breathe in and push out used-up air when you breathe out.

### Question 66

It's like explaining a big word to a friend: say it simply first, then share the fancy word so they can learn it too.

### Question 67

Objective is the stuff you can see and measure, like a temperature of 98.6 or a blood pressure number — not what the patient feels.

### Question 68

'CXR' is short for 'chest X-ray' — a picture of the area where your heart and lungs live.

### Question 69

An ECG is like listening to the heart's electrical 'song' to make sure it's beating in a steady rhythm.

### Question 70

'Fasting blood glucose' means 'check the sugar in your blood after you've skipped food so we get a clean number.'

### Question 71

'BP' is short for 'blood pressure,' the push of blood against your arteries.

### Question 72

'STAT' is like a fire-drill word — it means 'do this right now.'

### Question 73

If someone points to the lower-right part of their belly, you write down exactly 'lower-right belly,' not a guess.

### Question 74

'Ileum' and 'ilium' are like 'knight' and 'night' — they sound the same but mean totally different things.

### Question 75

'My' means muscle and 'algia' means pain, so myalgia is 'my muscles hurt.'

### Question 76

'Cardio' is the word for heart — that's why heart doctors are called cardiologists.

### Question 77

If someone is short of breath, the problem is with their breathing parts — the lungs and airways.

### Question 78

A kilogram is about 2.2 pounds, so to find kilograms you split the pounds into groups of 2.2.

### Question 79

If you can't read a note clearly, you ask the person who wrote it — you don't guess, because guessing could hurt someone.

### Question 80

You write down exactly what happened and what the patient said, like a careful reporter — you don't add your own guess.

### Question 81

'Hemat' means blood and 'uria' means pee — so hematuria is blood in the pee.

### Question 82

'Dyspnea' is the doctor-word for 'it's hard to breathe.'

### Question 83

Edema means extra fluid has pooled in a body part, making it puffy — like a sponge that has soaked up too much water.

### Question 84

'Cyanotic' means a blue-ish color, like when your lips look a little blue — a sign the body might not have enough oxygen.

### Question 85

'Cardio' means heart, so a cardiologist is a heart doctor; 'neuro' means nerve, so a neurologist is a brain-and-nerve doctor.
